segments.text:
This function belongs to the cross-check block that starts in line 555. A Markdown table is a group of text lines that start with `|`. The cells stand between the `|` characters.
- The first line of a table gives the column titles (`head`).
- A later line whose cells hold only the characters `-`, `:` and space is the separator line. It is skipped.
- Every other line becomes one dictionary from column title to cell text.
- A line that does not start with `|` ends the table.
The function returns a list with one entry per table.
segments.heading: Function `md_tables`: parse the Markdown tables of a text

segments.text:
`md_sections` (line 556) splits the text of FACTS.md at its headings. `SEC` maps a section number, for example `3.4`, to the text of that section.
- The script stops unless 11 sections exist and hold text. These are the sections that the cross-checks of lines 652 to 767 read.
- `NUM` is the regular expression for one number: an optional sign, digits, and an optional decimal part.
segments.heading: `SEC`: the sections of FACTS.md, and the number pattern `NUM`

segments.text: `col` returns the cell whose column title starts with the text `start`. The script stops unless exactly one column title of the row starts with that text. The callers use it for long titles. Example: line 703 finds the title `Distance of the nearest ends, GB/s (+ = 7200 MT/s row higher)` with the start `Distance of the nearest ends`.
segments.heading: Function `col`: one cell of a table row

segments.text:
`facts_row` reads all tables of one FACTS.md section in their order.
- It returns the first row for which the test function `where` is true.
- A test can read a column that the table of a row lacks. Python then raises `KeyError`, and the row is skipped.
- The script stops when no row passes the test.
segments.heading: Function `facts_row`: find one row of a FACTS.md table

segments.text:
- `rng_of` finds the first text of the form `number to number` in a table cell. It returns the two numbers as `Decimal`. The script stops when the cell holds no such text.
- `near` is the comparison that the cross-checks use for rates, distances and percent values. It converts both values to `Decimal`. It is true when they differ by at most the tolerance `tol` (the largest allowed difference).
segments.heading: Functions `rng_of` and `near`: read a range, compare two values

segments.text:
- `rng_of` reads the two numbers of the FACTS.md cell.
- `q` (line 90) rounds the computed lowest value and the computed highest value to the rounding step `tol`. The default is 0.01 (GB/s). A value exactly between two steps is rounded away from zero.
- The check passes when each rounded value differs from its FACTS.md number by at most `tol`. So a difference of 0.01 GB/s in the last digit still passes.
- `check` adds one PASS or FAIL line that prints both ranges. After a FAIL the script continues, and it does not write the page at the end.
segments.heading: Function `xc_range`: a computed range against a table cell

segments.text:
`xc_val` does the same for one value.
- It takes the first number of the cell, with its sign. The script stops when the cell holds no number.
- The computed value is rounded to `tol` and compared with `near`.
- The callers pass 0.01 for a rate in GB/s and 0.1 for a percent value.
segments.heading: Function `xc_val`: a computed value against a table cell

segments.text:
`xc_text` is for a value that FACTS.md gives in a sentence and not in a table cell.
- It collects every number of the section text that is followed by the unit, with at most one space between them.
- It takes the computed value without its sign and rounds it to `tol`.
- The check passes when at least one collected number differs from it by at most `tol`.
- The check does not test which sentence holds the number.
segments.heading: Function `xc_text`: a computed value against the text of a section

segments.text: `xc_text_range` collects every text of this form in the section: a number, the text `unit_mid`, the word `to`, a number. Example with `unit_mid` = ` %`: the text `30.5 % to 31.2`. The check passes when one collected pair of numbers differs from the two rounded computed values by at most `tol` each. As in `xc_text`, the place of the text inside the section is not tested.
segments.heading: Function `xc_text_range`: a computed range against the text of a section

segments.text:
`xc_drops` takes the lowest and the highest drop of a list and rounds each to 0.1 (percent).
- The drops of the list were computed with `drop` (line 417) from rates that this script had not rounded for printing.
- For a bwx12 pair, the two rates are values of `val`, rounded to 6 decimals (line 188).
- For part A, the two rates are medians. Each is the median of the 3 rates of one process, as the csv file holds them (2 decimals).
- The columns `Smallest drop` and `Largest drop` of the FACTS.md row give the two numbers to compare with.
- The check passes when each pair differs by at most 0.1 (percent).
segments.heading: Function `xc_drops`: computed drops against a table row

segments.text:
`T34` returns one row of the table in FACTS.md section 3.4. The column `Part` of that row starts with the first text, and its column `Pair` holds the second text. Six `xc_drops` calls compare the drops of `Q1` (line 430) with that table:
- part C: bwx12 kernel `read` directly after `oldread` (4 pairs), and directly after `asmread` (4 pairs),
- part L: `asmread` against `oldread` (6 pairs),
- part A: the 6 drops between the medians of two processes,
- control I (4 pairs) and F72d12 (2 pairs).
The table has 9 rows. Its three rows for `asmread` in part C have no check here. The saved output of a build shows 30.5 % to 31.2 % and 29.7 % to 31.1 % for part C, both computed and in FACTS.md [Ref5].
segments.heading: Cross-check of question Q1 with FACTS.md

segments.text:
`G33` returns the row of FACTS.md section 3.3 whose column `Group` starts with the given text.
- Three `xc_range` calls compare the lowest and the highest rate of a part C group with the column `Min to max` of its row. The groups are `read` after `oldread` (4 intervals), `read` after `asmread` (4 intervals) and all `oldread` intervals (8 intervals).
- The loop tests with `xc_text_range` that section 0 of FACTS.md (its Short version) holds four drop ranges, to 0.1 percent: the two of part C, the one of part L and the one of part A.

Part A, one set of comparisons per session and round (the 6 entries of `A_PAIRS`, line 451).
- `facts_row` finds the row of section 3.1 with the same `Session` and `Round`, in the table that has the column `New below old, %`.
- `xc_val` compares the median of the 3 intervals of `bw_old read` and the median of the 3 intervals of `bw_new read`, each to 0.01 GB/s.
- `xc_val` compares the drop between the two medians with the column `New below old, %`, to 0.1 percent.
- `g0` is the length of `CHECKS` before the loop. `grouped` (line 56) replaces the 18 lines of the loop by one line that counts the equal comparisons.

The same for the 12 pairs of part L (6), control I (4) and F72d12 (2).
- The row of section 3.2 is found by its column `Folder tag or row` and by the round. For F72d12 the text `F72d12` is used in place of the folder tag.
- Three values are compared: the `oldread` rate and the `asmread` rate of the pair (each the value of `val`, to 0.01 GB/s) and the drop of the pair (to 0.1 percent).
- `grouped` joins the 36 comparisons into one line.

`R42` returns one row of FACTS.md section 4.2. The column `Row` of that row starts with the given name, and its table has the column `Min to max, GB/s`. `C42` returns the comparison row for a 7200 MT/s row and an 8000 MT/s range.
- Lines 686 to 692 compare 7 computed ranges of the old read kernel: part A, the pool A-1 to A-3, part L, the pool L-1 to L-4, part C, F72d12 and control I.
- Lines 693 and 694 compare the median of part L and the median of the pool L-1 to L-4 with the column `Median, GB/s`.
Each computed range is the lowest and the highest value of `val` in its group of records (class `Rg`, line 192).
segments.heading: Cross-check of question Q2 with FACTS.md: old read kernel

segments.text:
Two comparisons with overlap: part A against the pool A-1 to A-3, and part C against the pool L-1 to L-4.
- The `check` call needs two things. The column `Wording` of the FACTS.md row must hold `no difference seen`. `wording` (line 481) must return the same text for the two computed ranges.
- `xc_val` compares `width_pct` of the 8000 MT/s pool (line 476) with the column `Width of the 8000 MT/s range`, to 0.1 percent. This width is the size that the test cannot exclude (est.).
The saved output of a build shows 1.2 % for part A and 1.0 % for part C [Ref5].

Part L against the pool L-1 to L-4. This is the one comparison of the old read kernel in which the two ranges do not overlap.
- The wording must be the text for a difference, both in the FACTS.md row and from `wording`.
- `L_OLD_NEAR` (line 489) is compared with the column `Distance of the nearest ends`. The value is negative: part L is the lower range.
- Three `xc_text` calls test that section 4.9 holds three values. The first is the difference of the two medians in GB/s. The second is the distance of the nearest ends in percent of the lower end of the 8000 MT/s range (line 491). The third is the difference of the medians in percent of the 8000 MT/s median (line 492).
- For F72d12 and for control I the check passes when the column `Overlap` reads `yes` and the computed range overlaps the pool.
The saved output of a build shows -1.24 GB/s, 6.27 GB/s, 0.3 % and 1.3 % [Ref5].

`R44` and `C44` do for section 4.4 what `R42` and `C42` do for section 4.2. `C44` requires that the cell `8000 MT/s range used` is exactly the given text, not only its start.
- Lines 714 to 717: the `asmread` ranges of part L, the pool L-1 to L-4, F72d12 and control I.
- Lines 718 to 720: part L against the pool. The wording must be the text for a difference. The distance of the nearest ends is the first value of `DIST["nearest"]` (line 504).
- Line 721: the distance by which F72d12 lies above row L-1 alone.
- Line 722 reads FACTS.md only: the column `Overlap` of F72d12 against the pool must read `yes`. Lines 495 and 496 asserted the computed side.
- Line 723: the distance by which control I lies above the pool.
The saved output of a build shows 12.48 GB/s for part L, 1.73 GB/s for F72d12 and 4.61 GB/s for control I [Ref5].
segments.heading: Cross-check of question Q2 with FACTS.md: load-only loop

segments.text:
New read kernel of part A (`bw_new read`), once per round (rule V3). `v` is the entry of `A_V3` for the round (line 509). The row comes from the table of section 4.3 that has the column `Wording by rule V3`.
- The range of the 6 intervals of rows A-1 and A-2 (`r8`) is compared with the column `8000 MT/s range of the round, GB/s`.
- The cell `7200 MT/s, session 1` must hold three texts of the form `rate (pass count)`. Their lowest and highest rate are compared with the range of the 3 intervals of session 1 (`r7`), to 0.01 GB/s.
- The cell `Wording by rule V3` must read `outside (above)`. Line 514 asserted the computed side.
- The distance of the nearest ends is compared with the first number of the column `Distance to the nearer end`.
- The pass counts in the two 8000 MT/s cells, sorted, must equal the list `p8` of the records.

Part C, `asmread` directly after `oldread` (2 intervals), against the `asmread` range of the pool L-1 to L-4. The row of section 4.5 gives the range in the column `Its range` and the distance of the nearest ends. Line 738 tests that section 4.5 holds the text `Insufficient data: no 8000 MT/s run of kernel read with bwx12`. The check tests only that this text is present.

The three visits of the part L line in the 7200 MT/s boot: F72d12, part L and control I.
- Line 739: the `asmread` span `VISIT_HI - VISIT_LO` (line 501) must stand in section 4.6 with the unit GB/s. The span is the highest value of the three visits minus the lowest value.
- Line 740: section 4.9 must hold the lowest and the highest value as a text of the form `X to Y`.
- Lines 741 to 743: the three kinds of distance in `DIST` must stand in section 4.6, each for part L above the 8000 MT/s pool and for part L above F72d12.
- Line 744: the same span for `oldread` (line 502) must stand in section 3.4.
The saved output of a build shows 26.03 GB/s for `asmread` and 7.59 GB/s for `oldread` [Ref5].

Old read kernel in part A.
- Two `xc_text` calls test that section 0 holds the width of the 7200 MT/s range (`A_OLD_W7`) and the width of the 8000 MT/s pool range (`A_OLD_W8`), both from line 527.
- The `check` call builds the text `N of its M intervals lie below that range and K lie above it` from the computed counts (lines 525 and 526). It passes when section 0 holds this text.
- `grouped` joins the 3 comparisons into one line.
segments.heading: Cross-check: range widths of part A, rows of runner bwx

segments.text:
Rows of the older runner bwx, for the note under Table 2. `X45` returns the cell `Min to max, GB/s` of a row of section 4.5.
- Lines 754 to 756: three ranges of the pool of the bwx datasets B7a, B7b, C3a and C3b: `read` at position 1, `read` at position 6 and `asmread` at position 2.
- Lines 757 to 761: the three distances of `X_ABOVE` (line 545), by which a part C group lies above one of these ranges. Two are searched in the text of section 4.5. The third is compared with a table cell.
- Lines 762 to 765: the four highest values of lines 546 to 549, searched in section 4.6.
- Line 766: the text for n, searched in section 4.6. The counts come from the records: 192 intervals of 24 processes (line 326).
`grouped` joins the 11 comparisons into one line.

`V` is the part `verdicts` of facts.json. The modules `facts_text.py` and `facts_text4.py` computed its values during a run of `build_facts.py`. `vrow` returns the entry of the list `q2_rows` with the given part, kernel, 7200 MT/s row and 8000 MT/s scope. The script stops unless exactly one entry matches.
segments.heading: Function `vrow`: one verdict record of facts.json

segments.text:
- The lowest and the highest value of both ranges and the distance `dist` must each differ from the field of the record by at most 0.001 GB/s. The computed values are not rounded before this comparison. `build_facts.py` wrote these fields of the record rounded to 0.001 GB/s.
- The computed overlap result must equal the field `overlap`.
- The number of intervals (`n`) and the number of processes (`np`) of both ranges must equal the fields of the record exactly.
- `check` adds one PASS or FAIL line.
segments.heading: Function `xv`: two computed ranges against a verdict record

segments.text:
Eleven `xv` calls. The list `q2_rows` of this facts.json has 42 entries, and these lines compare 11 of them [Ref2].
- Old read kernel: part A against the pool A-1 to A-3. Part L, part C, F72d12 and control I against the pool L-1 to L-4.
- `asmread`: part L, F72d12, control I, and part C directly after `oldread`, each against the pool L-1 to L-4.
- `bw_new read`: session 1 against rows A-1 and A-2 of the same round, for round 1 and for round 2.
The last argument is the computed distance of the nearest ends. It is written as 0 in the five calls whose ranges overlap.
segments.heading: Cross-check with the verdict records of facts.json

segments.text:
Question Q1, part C.
- For each of the two groups of the bwx12 kernel `read`, the script takes the one entry of `verdicts.q1_parts` with the part `C` and that group. It stops unless exactly one such entry exists.
- The lowest and the highest computed drop must differ from the fields `smallest_drop_pct` and `largest_drop_pct` by at most 0.01 (percent). The drops are not rounded before this comparison. The record holds both fields rounded to 0.01 percent.
- `grouped` joins the 13 comparisons of lines 787 to 803 into one line.

The record `verdicts.same_boot` of facts.json holds values for the three visits of the 7200 MT/s boot. The check passes when seven computed values differ from it by at most 0.001 GB/s each.
- The first is the `asmread` span `VISIT_HI - VISIT_LO`.
- The other six are the distances of `DIST`: nearest ends, medians and farthest ends, each above the 8000 MT/s pool and above F72d12.

The comment in line 811 starts the checks of raw files for the page section on the machine state. The reference helpers are defined first. `REFS` is the list of the reference entries of the page.
- `addref` stops the script when the path does not exist.
- It shortens the path to `R/...` or `S/...`. It appends the text `lines` in parentheses when one is given.
- It stores three values: the key, this path text and the note.
- The calls of `addref` stand in lines 1389 to 1474.
segments.heading: Function `addref`: one entry of the reference list

segments.text: `ref` returns the HTML text that the page carries at a place that cites references. The script stops unless each key has exactly one entry in `REFS`. The text holds each key between two characters with the code 0 (written `\x00`). The reference numbers are not known yet.
segments.heading: Function `ref`: a reference mark in the page text

segments.text:
`number_refs` runs once, on the text of the whole page (line 2784).
- `order` lists the keys in the order of their first mark in the page.
- `uncited` lists the keys of `REFS` that no mark names. They get the numbers after the cited ones.
- Every mark is replaced by a link with the text `[RefN]`.
- One list item per reference is built. The items replace the text `\x01REFLIST\x01` in the page.
- The function returns the page and `uncited`. Line 2792 adds a FAIL line when `uncited` is not empty.
segments.heading: Function `number_refs`: number the references by first use

segments.text: `GOLOG` and `GO2LOG` are the saved run logs of go.sh and go2.sh. `STATE_RE` is the regular expression for a state line. It captures 12 fields, and `state_lines` uses 8 of them. `SYSTEM_ACCOUNTS` names the 6 accounts that the script calls system accounts.
segments.heading: Raw-file checks for the machine state section: the two run logs

segments.text:
`state_lines` returns one dictionary per line that matches `STATE_RE`.
- Its first entries are the line number, the name of the line (for example `start` or `after T72A1`), the time, the boot id and MemTotal in kB.
- The other entries are the 1-minute load average, the number of logins (the number after the word `users`), the state of the marker file, and `users`.
- `users` maps an account name to its number of processes. It is read from the list after `processes per user:`. An entry of that list has the form `11 jhan` and ends with `;`.
segments.heading: Function `state_lines`: parse the state lines of a run log

segments.text:
Each `need` call stops the script when its fact does not hold. Every test from here to line 1139 is such a call. The one exception is the `check` call of line 1035.
- The log of go.sh holds 12 state lines, and the log of go2.sh holds 6.
- All 18 lines hold the boot id and the MemTotal value of `meta.rerun` in facts.json.
- All 18 lines show 0 logins and the marker state `absent`.
- Only `jhan`, `root` and the 6 system accounts own processes. Each system account owns exactly 1 process in every line.
- The process count of `jhan` is the same in all 18 lines. The process count of `root` is not tested. It is 985 to 1014 in these lines.
segments.heading: Hard assertions on the two run logs

segments.text:
- The go.sh log must hold 10 lines that start with `done ` (one per step of the rerun). Its last line must be `ALLDONE`. No line may start with `FAILED`.
- The go2.sh log must hold 2 lines that start with `done `. The other two conditions are the same.
- The times of the first and the last state line of each log must equal the start time and the end time that `meta.rerun` holds for go.sh and for go2.sh.

- `LAUNCH` maps a folder tag to its entry of `meta.launches`. That list must name the 12 steps of `STEPS` in this order.
- `BWX_FOLDERS` holds the result folders of the `oldread` records of part L, part C and control I. There must be 9 folders.
- In each of these folders, launches.txt must hold exactly one line that starts with `rc `, and this line must start with `rc 0 `. So each folder holds one process, and its exit status is 0.
- `check(True, ...)` adds a summary line that is always PASS. The script reaches this line only when every `need` call above it held. Each later block of raw-file checks up to line 1139 ends with such a line too.

segments.heading: Boot record `try6.txt` of the 7200 MT/s boot
segments.text:
`TRY6` is the path of try6.txt, and `t6` holds its lines. The script stops unless the record holds these facts:
- line 2 is the boot id of the rerun,
- line 4 is the MemTotal value of the rerun,
- line 7 holds the count 12 before the text `Configured Memory Speed: 7200 MT/s`, and `meta.rerun` gives 7200 MT/s too,
- line 5 ends with the Linux kernel message `ghes_edac: This system has 12 DIMM sockets.`,
- line 6 has the form `modules=N`.

- `TRY6_MODLINE` is the N of line 6. It is 24 in this file, and it is not the module count. Line 1170 compares it with the module list.
- `TRY6_UTC` is line 1. The script stops unless it is a time of 2026-11-17.
- The script does not read lines 3 and 8 of the file. Line 3 is the output of the tool `uptime`. Line 8 holds the text `hwerr=0`.
- The command that wrote try6.txt is known from a record of the AI agent (Claude Code) that ran it. By this command, `hwerr` is the number of lines with the text `Hardware error from APEI` in the Linux kernel log (tool `dmesg`). The record is the file `4a6b911c-1987-43f1-be61-e96fcfc7261d.jsonl`. It lies outside the project folder.
- The file was written at 20:02:21 (line 1), before the rerun started at 22:12:09.

`boots.txt` is the saved boot list of the journal. A row holds a boot number, a boot id without hyphens, and the first and the last time of the boot.
- The last row must have the number 0 and the boot id of the rerun.
- `BOOT_FIRST` and `BOOT_LAST` are the two times of day of this row (its 5th and its 9th field).
- The file time of boots.txt (the time of its last change), written as a UTC time of day, must equal `BOOT_LAST`. So `BOOT_LAST` is the time at which the list was saved. The boot continued after it: the state lines of the rerun hold the same boot id.
segments.heading: Why F72d12 belongs to the 7200 MT/s boot

segments.text:
- Lines 1 and 2 of the launches.txt of F72d12 must be the `launch` line and the `rc 0` line of the process `a6456`. They give the launch time `F_LAUNCH` and the end time `F_END`.
- The launch time and the 1-minute load average of that line must equal the fields `launch_utc` and `load1_at_launch` of the first F72d12 record.
- The time in line 1 of try6.txt must be before the launch. The launch and the end must lie from `BOOT_FIRST` to `BOOT_LAST`. `BOOT_LAST` must be before the first state line of go.sh.
- These times are compared as texts `HH:MM:SS`. The dates in the rows of boots.txt are not compared.
The saved output of a build shows the process from 20:02:36 to 20:03:37, inside 20:02:21 to 20:06:19 [Ref5].

`h-5.txt` holds saved journal lines of the 8000 MT/s boot. The loop keeps the lines of the Linux kernel that carry the tag `[Hardware Error]`.
- A message that starts with `Hardware error from APEI` opens a new record in `HW`: line number, time stamp, severity not yet set.
- A message that starts with `event severity:` sets the severity of the newest record.
- The other lines of a record are skipped.
- The script stops unless `HW` holds at least one record and every severity is `corrected`.
- The script reads no hardware error record of the 7200 MT/s boot. For the rerun the page says `Insufficient data` (line 2474).
- Lines 957 to 1032 count the records inside the time windows of the rows L-1 to L-4 and A-1 to A-3 only. No line counts them for the rows of the older runner bwx (the records of `OTHER`, line 333). The page says so (line 2562).
The comment names a review finding by its identifier. The file `review-w2.json` in `S` holds this finding.
segments.heading: Hardware error records in the journal of the 8000 MT/s boot

segments.text:
`k-5.txt` is the saved kernel log of the 8000 MT/s boot.
- `BOOT8_FROM` and `BOOT8_TO` are the times of its first and its last line. Both lines must start with `Nov`, the day and the time. The year 2026 and the month 11 are fixed text of the script.
- The log must hold exactly one line with `ghes_edac: This system has 12 DIMM sockets`.
- It must hold as many lines with `Hardware error from APEI` as `HW` has records.
- The first journal line must start with the time `BOOT8_FROM`.
- Every record of `EIGHT` and of `OTHER` (the used 8000 MT/s records, lines 310 and 333) must have a launch time after `BOOT8_FROM` and before `BOOT8_TO`.

- `launch_window` reads launches.txt of a result folder. It returns the launch time and the end time of the process with the given tag. The end time is the time of its line `rc 0`. The script stops unless the file holds exactly one `launch` line and one `rc 0` line for the tag.
- `hw_in` returns the records of `HW` of one day whose time of day lies from `t0` to `t1`. Both ends count as inside.
segments.heading: Functions `launch_window` and `hw_in`

segments.text:
The loop handles each process of the rows L-1 to L-4. It takes the processes from the `asmread` records (`B_L_ASM`, line 292).
- `launch_window` gives the launch time and the end time of the process. The launch time must equal the field `launch_utc` of the record.
- `HW_ROWS` stores, per row and tag, the two times, the day and the hardware error records inside this time window.
- `HW_L1` is the count for L-1. `HW_L2` holds the counts of the two processes of L-2. `HW_L34` is the total of L-3 and L-4.
- The script stops unless L-1 has at least 1 record, each L-2 process has at least 1, and L-3 and L-4 have 0.
The saved output of a build shows 2 records for L-1, 5 and 4 for L-2, and 0 for L-3 and L-4 [Ref5].
segments.heading: Hardware error records during the rows L-1 to L-4

segments.text:
Helpers for the rows A-1 to A-3, which ran in the 8000 MT/s boot too.
- `a_headers` returns the line number, the launch time and the text of every process header line of the csv file that a part A record names. The launch time is the text `HH:MM:SS` after the word `utc`. The script stops when a header line has none.
- `secs` converts a time `HH:MM:SS` to seconds since midnight.
segments.heading: Functions `a_headers` and `secs`

segments.text:
All `bw_old read` records of these rows must be of 2026-11-13. `HA1`, `HA2` and `HA3` are the header lists of the three csv files.
- The time window of A-1 and of A-2 runs from the first launch to the last launch in the file.
- The csv file of A-3 holds more processes than the 3 that the page uses. Its window runs from the launch of the first process used to the launch of the process after the last one used. `_fproc` (line 349) gives the place of a process in the file. The script stops unless the records name exactly 3 processes and the file holds a later process.
- The six times must be in order, so the three windows do not overlap.
- The script stops unless the journal holds 4 records from the first launch of A-1 to the end of the A-3 window. All 4 must lie inside the window of A-2, and none inside the windows of A-1 and A-3.
- Records before the first launch of A-1 and after the end of the A-3 window are not counted in these lines. The file `h-5.txt` holds 42 such records of 2026-11-13: 4 before (the last at 18:16:53, 28 s before that launch) and 38 after (the first at 20:59:34).
segments.heading: Hardware error records during the rows A-1 to A-3

segments.text:
The last process of A-1 and of A-2 has no later header line in its file. So no launch of a next process marks its end.
- In place of an end time the script requires that no record has a time from 1 s to 60 s after that launch.
- `HW_A2_T` holds the different times of day of the 4 records in A-2. The script stops unless these are 2 times with 2 records each.

Which processes of A-2 the 4 records lie in.
- The first time must be the launch second of the `bw_new read` process of round 1. The record field `launch_utc` and the header line of that process must both give this second.
- `a2_other` is the last process of the file that was launched at or before the second time. Exactly one must exist.
- Its header line gives the binary and the kernel. The script stops when the kernel is `read` or `all`. Its stop message calls such a process a read process.
- `check(True, ...)` adds the summary line.
The saved output of a build shows 2 records at 20:50:58 and 2 at 20:51:10. The second pair lies in a `bw_new write` process that was launched at 20:51:08 [Ref5].

`LOWEST_ASM` (line 520) is the record with the lowest `asmread` rate of the pool.
- The script stops unless it belongs to row L-2, process `p2add`.
- `t_rows` (line 124) returns the 120 T rows of this interval.
- `T_START` is the lowest value of their 10th field `t_start_s`. `T_END` is the highest value of their 11th field `t_end_s`. Both are seconds since the start of the process.
segments.heading: The interval with the lowest asmread rate of the pool

segments.text: `clock` rounds the seconds `add` to a whole number. A value exactly between two whole numbers is rounded up. It adds the result to the time `hms` and returns the new time as `HH:MM:SS`.
segments.heading: Function `clock`: add seconds to a time of day

segments.text:
- `LOW_T0` is the launch time of the process `p2add`, as launches.txt gives it (line 962).
- `LOW_FROM` and `LOW_TO` are the times of day at which the interval started and ended, to the nearest second (est.). The runner script rx.sh wrote the launch time in whole seconds, directly before it started the process. So both times can differ from the true times by about 1 s.
- `HW_LOW` holds the hardware error records of that day from `LOW_FROM` to `LOW_TO`. The script stops unless these are exactly 2 records with one time stamp.
- This is the only interval for which the script computes a start time and an end time. It does not test whether a record lies inside any other interval. The counts of lines 957 to 999 are for the time window of a whole process (rows L-1 to L-4) or of a whole row (A-1 to A-3).
The saved output of a build shows 2 records at 18:54:52, inside 18:54:51 to 18:54:55 [Ref5].
segments.heading: Hardware error records inside the lowest asmread interval

segments.text:
`rPL_asm_wo` (line 521) is the range of the pool without this one interval. It comes from 10 of the 11 `asmread` intervals.
- `rPL_asm_wo` is used only in line 522, in these lines and in one sentence of Table 5 (line 2567). Every other `asmread` comparison with the pool L-1 to L-4 uses `rPL_asm` or the list `P_L_ASM`, which hold all 11 intervals. So the lowest interval is not left out of the other results of the page.
- When FACTS.md holds a sentence of the form `Without this interval the pool spans X to Y GB/s`, the check compares both values to 0.01 GB/s.
- When FACTS.md holds no such sentence, the script adds a PASS line that says so.
- The second `check(True, ...)` adds the summary line of the journal checks.
`state_table` (line 2503) prints these facts in Table 5. The saved output of a build shows 298.61 to 309.17 GB/s on both sides, and 288.54 GB/s for the interval that is left out [Ref5].

`FW` is the result folder `fwtest-20261117`. `set_records` reads one file `set.txt`.
- It returns the pairs (name, answer) of every reply in the file that is marked as modified. Two forms of reply are read. The first is a text block with the lines `name: "..."`, `answer: "..."` and `modified: true`. The second is a JSON line that starts with `{"responses"`.
- It also returns the time of line 1 as `HH:MM:SS` in the 24-hour form. For this, line 1 must be a date line of 17 November 2026 with AM or PM. Example: line 1 of `set.txt` in the folder `x1` reads `Tue Nov 17 03:43:50 AM UTC 2026`. For another line 1 the time is `None`.
The comment names a second review finding of `review-w2.json`.
segments.heading: Function `set_records`: the changed settings of a `set.txt` file

segments.text: Four files are read: `set.txt` of the folders `x1`, `x2` and `revert` of `FW`, and `set.txt` of the folder `dimm7200-20261117`. The script stops unless `x1` holds one change, `TXREQ Min` to `1/4 L2 TQ`, and `x2` holds one change, `TXREQ Max` to `1/4 L2 TQ`.
segments.heading: Firmware settings: the changes that the result files hold

segments.text:
- `Q_BASE` is the settings list that was saved in the 8000 MT/s boot. `Q_REV` is the list that was saved after the revert (the step that set both values back).
- `orig` holds the values of `TXREQ Max` and `TXREQ Min` in `Q_BASE`. The revert must have changed exactly these two settings, to these values.
- The times of line 1 must be in the order `x1`, `x2`, revert.
- `canon` turns a list into sorted JSON texts. The two lists must have the same length and the same entries. The order of the entries is not compared.
- `Q_BASE` must hold exactly one setting `DIMM Frequency`, and its value must be `8000 MT/s`.
- The file time of `Q_BASE` must lie after `BOOT8_FROM` and before `BOOT8_TO`.

- `N_SET` is the number of entries of the settings list.
- `SAME_ORDER` tells whether the two lists are equal in their order too.
- `UNREAD` counts the entries whose answer is an error marker of the form `<Name: ...>` and not a value, per marker name. The script stops unless the marker names are exactly `ValueUnavailable` and `VStoreError`. For such an entry, line 1075 compares the marker text. It does not compare a value of the setting.
- `N_UNREAD` is the total.
The saved output of a build shows 1490 entries, of which 886 have no readable value [Ref5].

- `set.txt` of the folder `dimm7200-20261117` must hold one change: `DIMM Frequency` to `7200 MT/s`.
- `os.walk` finds every file with the name `set.txt` under `R`. The script stops unless these are exactly the 4 files above.
- `D72_T` is the file time of the `set.txt` of `dimm7200-20261117` as a UTC time of day. It must lie after the time of the revert and before the time in line 1 of try6.txt. Only the times of day are compared, not the dates.
- `check(True, ...)` adds the summary line.
The saved output of a build shows the two changes at 03:43:50 and 04:05:38, the revert at 04:13:19 and the file time 19:43:03 [Ref5].

The runner script rx.sh writes the process list of env.txt with the tool `ps`: sorted by %CPU, highest value first, and limited to the first 5 processes. `ps` computes %CPU as the CPU time that a process has used, divided by the time since the process started. So the value is an average over the life of the process.
- Line 1 of the file must be a date line of 17 November 2026 with AM or PM. `when` is its time as `HH:MM:SS` in the 24-hour form.
- Line 4 must be the title line with the words `USER`, `%CPU` and `COMMAND`. rx.sh writes the output of the tool `who` (one line per login) before the process list. So line 4 is the title line only when `who` printed no line.
- Each line from line 5 up to the first line that starts with `binary ` becomes one row: line number, user, %CPU as `Decimal`, command. Each of the 6 files read here holds 5 such rows.
- The script stops when there are fewer than 3 rows.
- The function returns `when` and the rows.
segments.heading: Function `proc_list`: the process list of an env.txt file

segments.text:
F72d12, the first of the three visits.
- `F_TOP` is the row of its process list with the highest %CPU. The script stops unless this is line 5 of the file, the command `pr/ttyAMA-1` of the user `root`.
- Line 7 of gaps.txt gives `BOOT7_KLOG`, the time of the first kernel log line of the 7200 MT/s boot. The script stops unless this line starts with `0 first=` and a time of 2026-11-17.
- The script takes only this time from the line. The same line holds a second time (20:06:34, after `last=`) and the text `hwerr=0`. The script does not read them.
- `F_AFTER_BOOT_S` is the launch time of F72d12 minus `BOOT7_KLOG`, in seconds. `F_ENV_BEFORE_S` is the launch time minus the time of the process list.
- Both must be above 0 s and below 60 s.
The saved output of a build shows 20 s and 5 s, and 51.6 %CPU for `pr/ttyAMA-1` [Ref5].
segments.heading: Start state of the three visits of the part L line

segments.text:
Part L and control I, the two later visits (5 steps).
- For each step, `proc_list` reads env.txt of the result folder of the step.
- The process list must have been written more than 0 s and less than 60 s before the first launch of the step (`first_launch` in `meta.launches`).
- `VISIT_ENV` keeps the path of env.txt and the highest %CPU of its list.
- The script stops unless the highest %CPU value of all 5 lists is below 1 %. %CPU is an average over the life of a process. So this test cannot show a short busy phase of a process that has run since the boot.
- `check(True, ...)` adds the summary line.
The saved output of a build shows at most 0.1 %CPU [Ref5].
